scenes.heading: Scientific notation
scenes.sub: Huge and tiny numbers made short
scenes.say: How do you write a number with ten zeros without losing count? Scientists use a trick called scientific notation: a short number times a power of ten.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A rider on a zip line slides along while the digits stay still
scenes.science: The index says how many places the decimal point moves
scenes.breaks: The point can slide either way, and when it passes the last digit you fill gaps with zeros.
scenes.say: Imagine the decimal point is a rider on a zip line, and the digits stay still. The power of ten tells the rider how far to slide. A positive index slides right and the number gets bigger. A negative index slides left and the number gets smaller.

scenes.heading: The form
scenes.say: Scientific notation is a times ten to the n. a must be at least one and less than ten, so there is one digit before the point. n is a whole number: positive for big numbers, negative for numbers less than one.
scenes.caption: Scientific notation is a × 10ⁿ. a must be at least 1 and less than 10, so there is one digit before the point. n is a whole number: positive for big numbers, negative for numbers less than 1.

scenes.heading: A small number
scenes.question: Write 0.000 0605 in scientific notation.
scenes.say: Write zero point zero zero zero zero six zero five in scientific notation. Start at the first non-zero digit, six, so a is six point zero five. Keep the zero in the middle. The point moves five places left, so the index is negative five. Count the moves, not the zeros!
scenes.caption: Write 0.000 0605 in scientific notation. Start at the first non-zero digit, 6, so a = 6.05. Keep the middle 0. The point moves 5 places left, so the index is −5. Count the moves, not the zeros!

scenes.heading: Multiplying
scenes.question: Calculate (4 × 10⁵) × (6 × 10³).
scenes.say: Multiply four times ten to the five by six times ten cubed. Numbers first: four times six is twenty-four. Powers: add the indices, ten to the eight. But twenty-four is too big, so make it two point four and add one to the index. Answer: two point four times ten to the nine.
scenes.caption: Multiply (4 × 10⁵) × (6 × 10³). 4 × 6 = 24. Add the indices: 10⁸. 24 is too big, so make it 2.4 and add 1 to the index. Answer: 2.4 × 10⁹.

scenes.heading: Which is bigger?
scenes.say: Which is bigger: one point two times ten to the negative two, or nine point nine times ten to the negative four? Look at the index first. Negative two is bigger than negative four, so the first number wins, even though nine point nine looks bigger.
scenes.caption: Which is bigger: 1.2 × 10⁻² or 9.9 × 10⁻⁴? Look at the index first. −2 is bigger than −4, so the first number wins, even though 9.9 looks bigger.

points: a × 10ⁿ with a from 1 up to (not incl.) 10
Count the moves, not the zeros
Multiply: add indices, then adjust a
scenes.say: Recap. Scientific notation is a times ten to the n, with one digit before the point. Big numbers get a positive index, small numbers a negative one. Count the moves of the point, not the zeros. When you multiply, add the indices and adjust a. Now try the practice questions!
